Construct a Multivariate Student t Distribution

Source: R/mvstudent_t_distrib.R
mvstudent_t1_distrib.Rd

Two families on \(\mathbb{R}^p\), differing in which matrix their parametrization describes: mvstudent_t1_distrib() parametrizes the scale matrix \(\Sigma\) and mvstudent_t2_distrib() its inverse \(\Sigma^{-1}\). Each carries a location vector of \(p\) free parameters, the matrix through a parameters7 parametrization, and a positive degrees-of-freedom parameter. The free values become ordinary scalar parameters, so the generics of the distrib class accept the object, with theta a flat named list of numbers; the distribution function and the quantile function signal an error. Both default to an unstructured matrix in the log-Cholesky parametrization, which has p * (p + 1) / 2 free values, and to a log link on nu.

Usage

mvstudent_t1_distrib(n_dim, sigma = NULL, link_nu = linkfunctions7::log_link())

mvstudent_t2_distrib(n_dim, omega = NULL, link_nu = linkfunctions7::log_link())

Arguments

n_dim

The dimension \(p\) of one observation. The value must be a single positive whole number, finite and at least 1. Any other value signals an error.

sigma

A parameters7 parametrization of the scale matrix, of dimension n_dim and of full rank. Defaults to parameters7::log_cholesky(n_dim). A rank-deficient parametrization is rejected because the density does not normalize.

link_nu

The link carrying the degrees of freedom to the unconstrained scale, a linkfunctions7::link object. Defaults to linkfunctions7::log_link(), which keeps \(\nu\) strictly positive at every point of the free scale.

omega

A parameters7 parametrization of the inverse scale matrix, of dimension n_dim and of full rank. Defaults to parameters7::log_cholesky(n_dim). It is the precision of the response only up to the factor \((\nu-2)/\nu\); see Details.

Value

An S7 object of class MvStudentT1Distrib or MvStudentT2Distrib, whose param is the parametrization supplied and whose inverted records which matrix param carries. Its params are mu1, ..., mup, the prefixed free names, then nu; n_params is p + param@n_free + 1; every params_bounds entry is \((-\infty, \infty)\) except that of nu, which is \((0, \infty)\); and every link is the identity except that of nu.

The two matrices

Each of the two matrices is neither a covariance nor a precision. \(\Sigma\) is the scale matrix, the matrix in the quadratic form of the density, and the moments are obtained from it by scaling in \(\nu\):

$$\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{\nu}{\nu-2}\,\Sigma \quad (\nu > 2), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)^{-1} = \frac{\nu-2}{\nu}\,\Sigma^{-1}.$$

So the matrix of mvstudent_t2_distrib() equals the precision of the response only up to the factor \((\nu-2)/\nu\), which is 2/3 at \(\nu = 6\); a coordinate named omega_log_L1 is a free value of \(\Sigma^{-1}\) and not of the precision. The prefixes follow the convention of mvgaussian1_distrib() and name which of the two matrices a free value builds.

For \(\nu \le 2\) the covariance does not exist while the density is well defined, and for \(\nu \le 1\) the mean does not exist either. For that reason mv_sigma() returns the scale matrix, which the parametrization carries and which exists at every admissible \(\nu\), and variance() returns the covariance, a moment, which is Inf in every entry for \(\nu \le 2\); mean() returns NaN for \(\nu \le 1\). A fit therefore runs at \(\nu = 1.5\).

Two readings carry over from the matrix to the response without a factor, because a positive multiple cancels out of a ratio:

  • the correlations of \(\Sigma\) are the correlations of \(Y\);

  • the partial correlations read off \(\Sigma^{-1}\), as \(-\Omega_{jk}/\sqrt{\Omega_{jj}\Omega_{kk}}\), are the partial correlations of \(Y\).

The conditional variance does not carry over. For a gaussian \(1/\Omega_{jj}\) is the conditional variance of \(Y_j\) given the rest; here it is the Schur complement of the scale matrix, so it is a conditional scale, and the conditional law of a \(t\) is itself a \(t\) whose scale carries a further factor depending on the conditioning values. mv_summary() names that quantity cscale_vj and not cvar_vj for this reason, as it names the diagonal quantities scale_sd_vj.

Which side to write a structure on

Where the matrix parametrization is closed under inversion the two families describe the same laws in different coordinates. Where it is not they are different models: mvstudent_t2_distrib(p, parameters7::ar1(p)) is the family whose inverse scale matrix has the entries \(\sigma^2\rho^{|i-j|}\), with \(\sigma^2\) the scale of ar1(), and it is a valid law. The AR(1) pattern on the scale matrix, in the family that parametrizes the inverse, is mvstudent_t2_distrib(p, parameters7::ar1_inv(p)), whose parametrization is that inverse.

Parameters

The location contributes mu1, ..., mup, the parametrization contributes its free values under the sigma_ prefix for the scale matrix and the omega_ prefix for its inverse, and nu comes last. The location and the matrix parameters are unconstrained and carry identity links; nu is positive and carries link_nu. Unlike mvgaussian1_distrib(), this family therefore has a link scale that differs from its parameter scale: under the default log link, scale = "link" applies the chain rule of the log link to every derivative in nu.

The weight of an observation

When a gaussian is fitted to data with a few outlying rows, the estimated covariance grows until it covers them. A \(t\) whose \(\nu\) is estimated does not: an observation at squared Mahalanobis distance \(q\) enters every derivative through the weight \(c = (\nu+p)/(\nu+q)\), which falls as \(1/q\). The gaussian is the limit \(\nu \to \infty\), where \(c \equiv 1\).

The expected information

The expected information has a closed form, obtained from the family's own scale mixture; see distrib_expected_hessian.MvStudentTDistrib() for the four blocks. fit_distrib() therefore rejects an approx argument on fisher_scoring() for this family, as it does for any family that computes its expected information exactly.

Reading a fit

For the scale parametrization, mv_summary() reports the square roots of the diagonal of the scale matrix, named scale_sd_v1, ..., scale_sd_vp because they are not standard deviations of the response, and the correlations, which are the response's as well. For the inverse parametrization it reports instead the conditional scales cscale_v1, ..., cscale_vp and the partial correlations pcor_vj_vk, which are the response's exactly.

Degrees of freedom far from the gaussian limit and close to it

Every quantity that depends only on \(\nu\) (the constant of the density and its derivatives, and the expected information in \(\nu\)) is computed by mvt_cp_d() and mvt_info_nunu() without the cancellation of the direct difference of gamma and polygamma functions, and the part that carries the data by mvt_h_d(); all of them vanish as \(\nu\) grows, while the terms of the direct forms do not.

The response

The response is an \(n \times p\) matrix with one row per observation. A plain vector of length \(p\) is read as a single observation. A parameter may not vary from observation to observation.

The distribution

$$f(y) = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu+p}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)(\nu\pi)^{p/2}\lvert \Sigma \rvert^{1/2}}\left(1 + \frac{q}{\nu}\right)^{-(\nu+p)/2}, \qquad q = (y-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(y-\mu)$$ on \(y \in \mathbb{R}^{p}\), with $$\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu \; (\nu > 1), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{\nu}{\nu-2}\Sigma \; (\nu > 2).$$

Notation

\(\mu\) is the location, \(\Sigma\) the scale matrix, \(\nu\) the degrees of freedom, \(p\) the dimension of one observation and \(q\) the squared Mahalanobis distance of an observation from the location. \(\eta\) is the free vector of the matrix parametrization.

See also

mvgaussian1_distrib() for the limiting family, student_t1_distrib() for the one-dimensional case, mv_marginal.MvStudentTDistrib() for a marginal, which keeps the same \(\nu\), parameters7::inverse_of() for writing a structure on the other side, and fit_distrib() to estimate one.

Examples

d <- mvstudent_t1_distrib(2)
d
#> Distribution: Multivariate Student T [2d, Sigma=log_cholesky]
#> Type:         Continuous, 2-dimensional
#> Dimensions:   multivariate
#> 
#> Parameters:
#>   mu1          (location)           | Link: identity   | Domain: (-Inf, Inf)
#>   mu2          (location)           | Link: identity   | Domain: (-Inf, Inf)
#>   sigma_log_L1 (scale)              | Link: identity   | Domain: (-Inf, Inf)
#>   sigma_log_L2 (scale)              | Link: identity   | Domain: (-Inf, Inf)
#>   sigma_L2.1   (scale)              | Link: identity   | Domain: (-Inf, Inf)
#>   nu           (degrees of freedom) | Link: log        | Domain: (0, Inf)

theta <- list(mu1 = 0.5, mu2 = -0.3, sigma_log_L1 = 0.1,
              sigma_log_L2 = -0.2, sigma_L2.1 = 0.4, nu = 6)

# The parametrization carries the scale matrix; the covariance is a moment
# and is larger by nu / (nu - 2).
mv_sigma(d, theta)
#>           v1        v2
#> v1 1.2214028 0.4420684
#> v2 0.4420684 0.8303200
all.equal(variance(d, theta), (6 / 4) * mv_sigma(d, theta))
#> [1] TRUE

# For nu <= 2 the covariance is infinite and the density is finite; for
# nu <= 1 the mean does not exist.
theta$nu <- 1.5
c(density = distrib_pdf(d, c(0, 0), theta), variance = variance(d, theta)[1, 1])
#>   density  variance 
#> 0.1018402       Inf 
theta$nu <- 0.8
c(density = distrib_pdf(d, c(0, 0), theta), mean = mean(d, theta)[1])
#>    density    mean.v1 
#> 0.08456772        NaN 

# At four units of scale from the location, a t at nu = 6 has a far larger
# density than a gaussian with the same matrix.
theta$nu <- 6
g <- mvgaussian1_distrib(2)
c(t = distrib_pdf(d, c(4.5, -4.3), theta),
  gaussian = distrib_pdf(g, c(4.5, -4.3), theta[1:5]))
#>            t     gaussian 
#> 1.413233e-05 6.118878e-14 

# The other parametrization carries the inverse scale matrix, and the prefix
# of its free values names it.
o <- mvstudent_t2_distrib(2)
o@params
#> [1] "mu1"          "mu2"          "omega_log_L1" "omega_log_L2" "omega_L2.1"  
#> [6] "nu"          

# Its matrix is the precision of the response only up to (nu - 2) / nu.
th_o <- list(mu1 = 0, mu2 = 0, omega_log_L1 = 0.1,
             omega_log_L2 = -0.2, omega_L2.1 = 0.4, nu = 6)
Om <- parameters7::param_value(o@param, unlist(th_o)[3:5])
all.equal(unname(solve(variance(o, th_o))),
          unname((6 - 2) / 6 * unclass(Om)))
#> [1] TRUE

# The correlations are the response's exactly: a positive multiple cancels
# out of a ratio.
all.equal(cov2cor(mv_sigma(o, th_o)), cov2cor(variance(o, th_o)))
#> [1] TRUE
